claim: Volatility clusters: a high-vol month tends to be followed by another (AR(1) coefficient of monthly log realised variance 0.6444, 95% CI 0.507 to 0.7818).
evidence: log_rv_cal / calendar months 2003–2025 / ar1_rho: 0.6444 [0.507, 0.7818] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC z, z = 9.19, p = 3.9e-20
caveat: Persistence fades fast: see the half-life and autocorrelations in the summary.

claim: Volatility shocks fade: realised variance is mean-reverting (augmented Dickey–Fuller statistic -5.933 rejects a unit root).
evidence: log_rv_cal / calendar months 2003–2025 / adf_stat: -5.933, ADF (constant, 1 lags by AIC), H0: unit root, p = 2.4e-07

claim: Realised volatility has risen gradually since 2003 (trend in log realised variance 0.001466 per year, 95% CI -0.03897 to 0.0419).
reasons: calendar months 2003–2025: CI [-0.03897, 0.0419] does not exclude 0
evidence: log_rv_cal / calendar months 2003–2025 / trend_slope_per_year: 0.001466 [-0.03897, 0.0419] (Newey–West (12 lags)), HAC z, z = 0.07, p = 0.94
fallback: Say: there is no evidence of a long-run trend in realised volatility since 2003; it moves in spikes that fade, around a stable level.

claim: Volatility jumps up faster than it falls: month-to-month changes in log realised variance are positively skewed (skewness 0.3321, 95% CI 0.03249 to 0.6523).
evidence: dlog_rv_cal / calendar months 2003–2025 / skewness: 0.3321 [0.03249, 0.6523] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.0378
fallback: Say: month-to-month changes in volatility lean towards sharp rises (positive sample skewness), but the effect does not survive the multiple-testing correction; show it on the chart rather than claim it.

claim: In raw variance the seller earns more when the VIX starts high: VIX > 25 months pay 0.007015 more than VIX ≤ 15 months (95% CI -0.04863 to 0.04586).
reasons: VIX > 25 minus VIX ≤ 15: CI [-0.04863, 0.04586] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_var / VIX > 25 minus VIX ≤ 15 / diff_mean_high_minus_low: 0.007015 [-0.04863, 0.04586] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.77
caveat: Known-at-t buckets, in-sample: a description, not an out-of-sample rule.
fallback: Say: the raw premium is larger on average in VIX > 25 months, but the difference is not significant: high-VIX months also contain the biggest losses.

claim: As a share of implied variance the premium is smaller when the VIX starts high: VIX > 25 minus VIX ≤ 15 = -15.1% (95% CI -65.9% to 23.1%).
reasons: VIX > 25 minus VIX ≤ 15: CI [-0.6591, 0.2311] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_scaled / VIX > 25 minus VIX ≤ 15 / diff_mean_high_minus_low: -0.1506 [-0.6591, 0.2311] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.50
caveat: Known-at-t buckets, in-sample: a description, not an out-of-sample rule.
fallback: Say: the point estimate is lower in high-VIX months, but we cannot distinguish it from the low-VIX premium.

claim: Even when the VIX starts high (VIX > 25) the seller wins on average: mean scaled payoff 9.8% (95% CI -28.5% to 48.1%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / VIX > 25 / mean: 0.09792 [-0.2855, 0.4813] (Newey–West (6 lags, within bucket)), HAC t, t = 0.50, p = 0.62
fallback: Say: in VIX > 25 months the seller still wins most months (see the win rate), but the average is not significantly above zero because those months hold the largest crashes.

claim: The premium is larger when the VIX sits well above recent realised vol: gap > 5 pts months pay 17.4% of implied variance more than gap ≤ 0 pts months (95% CI -15.7% to 52.0%).
reasons: gap > 5 pts minus gap ≤ 0 pts: CI [-0.1565, 0.5203] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_scaled / gap > 5 pts minus gap ≤ 0 pts / diff_mean_high_minus_low: 0.1739 [-0.1565, 0.5203] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.33
caveat: Known-at-t buckets, in-sample: a description, not an out-of-sample rule.
fallback: Say: the point estimate is larger when the VIX is well above recent realised vol, but with only a few dozen inverted months the gap is not significant.

claim: The scaled premium has shrunk over time: linear trend -0.4% of implied variance per year (95% CI -2.1% to 1.3%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / trend_slope_per_year: -0.004069 [-0.02097, 0.01283] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC z, z = -0.47, p = 0.64
caveat: A linear trend through 35 years of spiky data; pre-2003 VIX values are back-calculated. Show the rolling chart next to it.
fallback: Say: there is no significant evidence that the premium is shrinking once we correct for multiple testing.

claim: The premium more than pays for crashes: for the seller to break even, a loss the size of March 2020 would have to strike once every 2.195 years (95% CI 1.624 to 3.818), measured as a share of implied variance; it struck once in 22 years.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / breakeven_years_between: 2.195 [1.624, 3.818] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), one-sided exact Poisson P(N ≤ observed) at the lower CI bound of the break-even rate (conservative), p = 0.0201
caveat: In-sample. By construction the break-even frequency exceeds the observed one whenever the mean payoff is positive; the test asks how unlucky we would have to have been to see so few crashes. 1987 is outside the sample, and a crash bigger than any seen since 2003 would change the answer.

claim: In raw variance too, break-even needs a loss the size of March 2020 once every 6.104 years (95% CI 3.783 to 26.81); it struck once in 22 years.
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 2003–2025 / breakeven_years_between: 6.104 [3.783, 26.81] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), one-sided exact Poisson P(N ≤ observed) at the lower CI bound of the break-even rate (conservative), p = 0.80
caveat: In-sample. By construction the break-even frequency exceeds the observed one whenever the mean payoff is positive; the test asks how unlucky we would have to have been to see so few crashes. 1987 is outside the sample, and a crash bigger than any seen since 2003 would change the answer.
fallback: Say: in raw variance the margin is thinner: break-even needs a March 2020-sized loss about every 6 years against once in 22 years; with so few crashes observed we cannot rule out that they are that frequent.
